\title{Review scheduling under a fixed budget in simulated forgetting
models: a model-based advantage that depends on model knowledge and on
the setting}
\author{Mohamed Bechir Kefi}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Abstract}\label{abstract}

Model-based spaced-repetition schedulers review the items with the
lowest predicted recall. Whether this beats simple equal spacing under a
fixed number of reviews depends on the memory model as much as on the
schedule. We compared five schedules (uniform, expanding, massed,
Leitner and a greedy lowest-predicted-recall scheduler) in a simulation
of exponential and power-law forgetting with multiplicative retrieval
updates, under an exactly matched budget of 200 reviews for 50 synthetic
items, with two parameters calibrated to public Duolingo traces. Three
experiments were frozen before any confirmatory run (18,550 runs, none
excluded). At the central setting, with a test 281 days after a 28-day
study window, an oracle greedy scheduler raised mean modelled recall
over uniform review by 0.0162 (95\% bootstrap interval 0.0110 to 0.0213;
50 paired simulated learners), while lowering the already small share of
items above 0.9 (0.0200 to 0). On power-law learners, the same scheduler
using a misspecified exponential model gained 0.0085 (interval -0.0026
to 0.0195), which the frozen rule classifies as practically equivalent
to uniform; exploratory checks show that this classification is fragile.
Across a 72-cell sweep, the arm ranking changed in 70 cells and the best
arm was most often massed review (29 cells), which places every review
in the last four sessions. Within these models no schedule is best in
general; the answer depends on forgetting model, budget, retention
interval and the scheduler's knowledge. Neither model predicts real
first-review recall better than a constant, so none of this is a claim
about human learners.

\section{Keywords}\label{keywords}

spaced repetition; forgetting curves; review scheduling; simulation
study; model misspecification; protocol freezing

\section{1. Introduction}\label{introduction}

Learning software decides when a learner should see an item again. Two
families of rules are common: fixed rules, which space reviews by a
timetable, and adaptive rules, which use the learner's history.
Model-based adaptive rules go further: they estimate each item's current
recall probability under a forgetting model and review the items that
are about to be forgotten. Tabibian et al.~(2019) derive such a rule as
the optimal review intensity under a forgetting model and a review cost.
Settles and Meeder (2016) fit a half-life regression model to Duolingo
traces for the same purpose.

A model-based scheduler is only as good as its model. In a simulation,
the experimenter chooses the true model and can give the scheduler that
same model, which makes the comparison easy to win. This study asks how
much of the advantage of a model-based scheduler survives three changes:
a fixed, exactly matched review budget; a scheduler whose model is
wrong; and a sweep over settings that a reader could reasonably have
chosen instead.

\textbf{Research question.} Which review schedule maximizes modelled
delayed recall of a set of synthetic items under a fixed study budget (a
fixed total number of review events within a fixed study window)?

\textbf{Hypotheses.} The primary contrast is greedy minus uniform at the
central setting under exponential forgetting (EXP-001), with H0 that the
mean paired difference is 0 and a two-sided H1; the directional
prediction, stated before the run, was greedy above uniform. EXP-002 is
the principal invalidation test: it repeats the contrast on power-law
learners with a scheduler whose model is either matched or misspecified.
EXP-003 is a descriptive sweep without hypothesis tests.

\textbf{Contributions.} The contributions are limited to what the
evidence supports:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A budget-matched simulation comparison of five review schedules under
  two published forgetting-model families, with a protocol,
  configurations and analysis code frozen and hashed before any
  confirmatory output (18,550 runs).
\item
  A direct test of how much of the model-based advantage depends on the
  scheduler knowing the true model (EXP-002), with a pre-stated
  interpretation rule, and exploratory evidence on how robust that
  rule's outcome is.
\item
  A 72-cell descriptive sweep showing that the ranking of schedules
  depends on forgetting model, budget, retention interval and item
  distribution, including settings where the model-based scheduler is
  worse than equal spacing.
\item
  A calibration of the simulated item population's time scale to public
  first-review recall data, together with the finding that neither
  forgetting model predicts that recall better than a constant, which
  bounds every other result.
\end{enumerate}

No novelty is claimed relative to the literature that was not read
(section 2).

\section{2. Related work}\label{related-work}

The related-work base is small and every source is labelled by how much
of it was read (\texttt{research/literature\_review.md}). This is not a
systematic review.

\textbf{Forgetting models and optimal scheduling (content read).}
Tabibian et al.~(2019; content read in arXiv:1712.01856 v2) state an
exponential recall model \(m(t) = \exp(-n\Delta)\) and a power-law model
\(m(t) = (1 + \omega\Delta)^{-n}\), with a multiplicative update of the
forgetting rate \(n\) after a success or failure. Under a quadratic loss
with a review cost, they derive an optimal review intensity that grows
as predicted recall falls, and compare it with uniform and threshold
baselines. MEMORY uses these model forms and update directly. It differs
in two ways: the budget is a hard count of review events rather than a
priced intensity, and the scheduler's knowledge of the model is varied
on purpose.

\textbf{Half-life regression and classic schedules (content read).}
Settles and Meeder (2016; abstract and sections 1 to 3.3 read) model
recall as \(p = 2^{-\Delta/h}\) with a learned half-life \(h\), and
describe the Pimsleur graduated-interval method and the Leitner box
system (intervals of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days). The expanding and Leitner
arms of this study follow those descriptions. Their engagement and
error-reduction findings are theirs and are not used here.

\textbf{Spacing and retention interval (abstract read only).} The
abstract of Cepeda et al.~(2006) reports, from a quantitative synthesis
of 839 assessments in 317 experiments, that the inter-study interval
that maximizes retention increases with the retention interval. This
motivated the retention-interval factor of EXP-003. Only the abstract
was read; no further claim about that work is made.

\textbf{Leitner queueing model (abstract read only).} Reddy et
al.~(2016; arXiv:1602.07032, abstract read) model the Leitner system as
a queueing network. It is related work for the Leitner arm and is not
used for any result.

\textbf{Not read.} Wixted and Ebbesen (1991), Averell and Heathcote
(2011), Pavlik and Anderson (2005), Ye et al.~(2022) and Cepeda et
al.~(2008) were identified at metadata level only. They are relevant
(the form of forgetting curves, alternative memory models,
optimal-control scheduling) but are not cited for content, and the study
cannot say whether its comparison already exists in them.

\textbf{Relation to prior work.} The study is an extension of published
model families, not a new memory model and not a replication of any
experiment. Its original part is the design: a hard budget, matched
seeds, a pre-stated invalidation test for the scheduler's model
knowledge, and a sweep reported in full.

\section{3. Background and formal
model}\label{background-and-formal-model}

\textbf{Time and items.} Time \(t\) is in days. Review sessions occur at
integer days \(1, \dots, D-1\) of a study window \([0, D)\); every item
is first studied at day 0 (encoding, outside the budget). The delayed
test is at \(T_{test} = D - 1 + RI\), where \(RI\) is the retention
interval after the last session. A simulated learner holds \(N\) items.

\textbf{Forgetting.} With \(\Delta = t - t_{r,i}\) the time since item
\(i\) was last reviewed and \(n_i\) its current forgetting rate, the
true recall probability is

\[m_i(t) = \exp(-n_i \Delta) \quad \text{(exponential)}, \qquad m_i(t) = (1 + \omega\Delta)^{-n_i} \quad \text{(power law)}.\]

\textbf{Retrieval update.} At a review, the outcome is
\(r \sim \text{Bernoulli}(m_i(t))\). A success sets
\(n_i \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,n_i\) and a failure
\(n_i \leftarrow (1+\beta)\,n_i\); in both cases
\(t_{r,i} \leftarrow t\). Items within a session are processed in
ascending index order. In this model a review's effect on \(n_i\)
depends only on its outcome, not on the gap since the last review;
spacing matters only through the success probability at the review and
the time from the last review to the test.

\textbf{Item difficulty.} Initial half-lives \(h_i(0)\) are homogeneous
(\(h_0\)), lognormal (\(\log h_i(0) \sim N(\log h_0, \sigma^2)\)) or
bimodal (an even mixture of \(h_0/3\) and \(3h_0\)). The exponential
rate is \(n_i(0) = \ln 2 / h_i(0)\); the power-law exponent is set so
that the initial half-life is the same,
\(n_i(0) = \ln 2 / \ln(1 + \omega h_i(0))\).

\textbf{Primary metric.} Delayed modelled recall
\(R = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i m_i(T_{test})\), the learner's mean true-model
recall probability at the test, in probability units. It is the exact
model probability, not a Bernoulli draw. Secondary metrics include
observed recall (one Bernoulli test draw per item), mastery share
(fraction of items with \(m_i(T_{test}) \ge 0.9\)), minimum and
10th-percentile item recall, scheduler calibration error, peak daily
load and sessions used.

\textbf{Complexity.} One run costs \(O(D \cdot N \log N)\) operations (a
sort of \(N\) items per session for the adaptive arms); a run took a few
milliseconds.

\section{4. Methods}\label{methods}

\subsection{4.1 Design and protocol
registration}\label{design-and-protocol-registration}

The study protocol (\texttt{research/protocol.md}) and three experiment
protocols were frozen by the owner before any confirmatory run. Version
1.0 was frozen on 2026-11-24 and superseded the same day by version 1.1
after a pre-data amendment (section 4.2); no confirmatory run was made
under v1.0. The SHA-256 of each protocol and of each canonical
configuration is stored in \texttt{research/freeze.json}; the run
command refuses any confirmatory configuration whose hashes differ (exit
3). The protocol was not registered with an external registry;
``frozen'' means hashed and committed in the project repository before
the runs.

Before the freeze, exploratory probes at the draft setting (initial
half-life 1 day) had computed the primary contrast on seeds disjoint
from the confirmatory ones, with greedy below uniform (PROBE-001:
-0.0286, interval -0.0349 to -0.0226). These values are disclosed in the
freeze record. The draft setting was replaced by the calibration and
amendments below, which were set by the owner's approvals and by rules
written before the computations they govern, not chosen from these
values.

\subsection{4.2 Simulated learners, calibration and the central
setting}\label{simulated-learners-calibration-and-the-central-setting}

\textbf{Calibration (CAL-001).} Two parameters of the item population
were fitted to public data: DS01, the Duolingo spaced-repetition traces
of Settles (2017, Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/DVN/N8XJME, CC BY-NC
4.0). The method was committed before the fit. Rows where the learner
had seen the word exactly once before measure recall at the first
review. Learners were split by a hash of their identifier; per-word
half-lives were fitted by maximum likelihood on the calibration split
(738 eligible words, 1 at a boundary). The median gave \(h_0 = 54.0\)
days and a robust spread \(\sigma = 0.759\). The validation split gave
55.2 days and 0.721, within the stability rule. The real data sets only
these two values; it never compares schedules.

\textbf{Model fit (CAL-002).} On held-out first-review recall (427,005
trials), the mean log-loss per trial was 0.328 for a constant predictor,
0.549 for the best exponential curve and 0.428 for the best power-law
curve. Neither forgetting model beats the constant: observed recall
stays near 0.9 at every delay (0.912 below one hour, 0.868 at 30 days or
more), which a curve starting at \(p(0) = 1\) cannot represent.

\textbf{Central setting.} \(N = 50\), \(D = 28\), \(k = 4\) reviews per
item (budget \(B = 200\)), \(h_0 = 54.0\) days, lognormal items with
\(\sigma = 0.759\), \(\alpha = 0.4\), \(\beta = 0.6\), \(\omega = 1\)
per day. \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\omega\) are planning values, not
estimates. With \(RI = 7\) days the uniform baseline sat near the
ceiling (mean \(R\) 0.959, PROBE-005), where differences are compressed.
Under an owner-approved rule written before it was applied (protocol
16.2), the central retention interval was moved, using the uniform arm
alone on exploratory seeds, to the value whose baseline recall was
closest to 0.55: \(RI = 281\) days (baseline 0.550; RI-001). No other
arm and no contrast was computed for this choice. The central cell
therefore describes recall about nine months after a four-week course.

\subsection{4.3 Schedules and baseline}\label{schedules-and-baseline}

All arms place exactly \(B\) reviews in sessions 1 to 27, at most one
review per item per session.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{uniform} (baseline): each item gets \(k\) equally spaced
  reviews, staggered by item index.
\item
  \texttt{expanding}: \(k\) reviews with gaps doubling, scaled to end at
  the last session (Pimsleur-style).
\item
  \texttt{massed} (negative control): all \(k\) reviews in the last
  \(k\) sessions.
\item
  \texttt{leitner}: five boxes with intervals 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days;
  success promotes, failure demotes to box 1.
\item
  \texttt{greedy}: each session reviews the items with the lowest
  predicted recall under the scheduler's model.
\end{itemize}

The adaptive arms share a fixed daily capacity
\(c_s = \lfloor sB/27 \rfloor - \lfloor (s-1)B/27 \rfloor\), which sums
exactly to \(B\), and first review any item not yet reviewed since
encoding. \texttt{uniform} is the baseline because it is the simplest
schedule that spends the budget and spaces practice. In EXP-001 the
greedy scheduler knows the true model and each item's initial half-life
(an oracle). In EXP-002, \texttt{greedy-power} has the true power-law
model and \texttt{greedy-exp} assumes exponential forgetting with the
same initial half-lives; both still receive the true initial half-lives.

\subsection{4.4 Metrics and statistical
analysis}\label{metrics-and-statistical-analysis}

The unit of analysis is the simulated learner (one seed); item outcomes
within a learner are averaged first. Arms are matched by common random
numbers: for a seed, every arm sees the same item difficulties and the
same pre-drawn uniform numbers per item and review index. For each arm
and seed the paired difference to \texttt{uniform} is computed; the mean
is reported with a 95\% percentile bootstrap interval over seeds (10,000
resamples, bootstrap seed 20261124) and a paired t interval as a
cross-check.

\textbf{Decision rule (frozen).} For a 95\% bootstrap interval of the
paired difference: entirely above 0, the difference is above zero;
entirely below 0, below zero; containing 0 and inside
\([-0.02, +0.02]\), practically equivalent; otherwise inconclusive.
Secondary contrasts use a Holm adjustment over the contrasts of the
family for any statement of difference.

\textbf{EXP-002 interpretation rule (frozen).} If EXP-001 shows a
positive difference, and either H0b (greedy-exp equals uniform) is not
rejected with its interval inside \(\pm 0.02\) or its interval lies
entirely below 0, the EXP-001 advantage is declared dependent on model
knowledge. Readings left implicit in the protocols (``positive
difference'' means the bootstrap interval is above 0; ``not rejected''
means a Holm-adjusted paired t p-value of at least 0.05 over the two
EXP-002 primary contrasts) were fixed in code and in decision D-015
before any confirmatory output existed.

\textbf{EXP-003 (descriptive).} Per cell, arm means and unadjusted 95\%
bootstrap intervals of arm minus uniform; the rank order of arms by mean
\(R\); a rank reversal is any pair of arms ordered differently from
EXP-001; the share of seeds in which each arm ranks first. Two
expectations were stated in advance and are not tested: E1,
\texttt{massed} improves relative to \texttt{uniform} as \(RI\)
decreases; E2, the greedy advantage is smallest for homogeneous items.

\subsection{4.5 Implementation, seeds and compute
budget}\label{implementation-seeds-and-compute-budget}

The simulator is a NumPy package (\texttt{src/memory\_research/}) with
234 passing tests at the run revision, covering probability bounds,
exact budgets, event ordering, known curve values and a differential
check against a reference simulator. A separate check computed every
metric and statistic on hand-solved cases (METRICVAL-001: 38 checks, 0
failed). EXP-001 and EXP-002 use seeds 1000 to 1049; EXP-003 uses a
disjoint block of 50 seeds per retention interval (3000 to 3049, 3100 to
3149, 3200 to 3249 and 3300 to 3349), so its retention-interval cells
are independent samples. All runs were executed once, at clean revision
\texttt{d4a793d}, on an Apple M1 Pro laptop (macOS 15.3.1, Python
3.12.1, NumPy 2.5.4), at zero cost. Wall-clock time was 0.603 s for
EXP-001 (250 runs), 0.907 s for EXP-002 (300 runs) and 36.063 s for
EXP-003 (18,000 runs), against caps of 10, 10 and 90 minutes.

\subsection{4.6 Exploratory versus confirmatory
work}\label{exploratory-versus-confirmatory-work}

EXP-001 and EXP-002 are confirmatory. EXP-003 is a confirmatory run of a
descriptive experiment: its counts are reported, not tested. Everything
labelled SENS-001 in this manuscript is exploratory and post hoc: it was
specified after the confirmatory results were seen (script committed at
\texttt{2e8cf05} before it was run), it uses committed raw outputs and
new exploratory seeds 5000 to 5049, and it never changes a frozen
verdict. The calibration and selection runs (CAL-001, CAL-002, RI-001,
PROBE-001 to PROBE-009) are exploratory design inputs.

The primary interval lies entirely above 0, so the directional
prediction is supported under the frozen rule. The effect is small:
0.0162 on a baseline of 0.5327, a relative change of 0.0303, with
standardized paired effect \(d_z\) 0.8674. The upper end of the interval
(0.0213) is just above the 0.02 margin. The standard deviation of the
paired differences, 0.0186, is well below the 0.07 adequacy threshold of
the protocol, so 50 seeds were sufficient.

\textbf{Metric choice.} The direction depends on the metric (Table 2).
Greedy raises the weakest items strongly and the observed (Bernoulli)
recall difference has an interval that contains 0. Mastery share
reverses: no item reaches 0.9 under greedy (0.0000) against 0.0200 under
uniform. Under the protocol's sensitivity rule, the EXP-001 conclusion
is restricted to mean recall. The reversal is formally decisive but
small in absolute terms: 0.0200 of 50 items is one item per learner on
average.

(exploratory).} The EXP-003 cell with the central setting (C044,
independent seeds 3300 to 3349) gave greedy minus uniform 0.0167
{[}0.0113, 0.0218{]} with the same rank order as EXP-001. SENS-001
re-simulated the central setting on seeds 5000 to 5049 and gave 0.0193
{[}0.0147, 0.0236{]}. On the confirmatory learners, the recorded recall
at shorter retention intervals also favours greedy: 0.0076 {[}0.0060,
0.0093{]} at \(RI = 1\), 0.0189 {[}0.0159, 0.0221{]} at 7 and 0.0392
{[}0.0353, 0.0431{]} at 30 days. The direction of the primary result is
therefore not an artefact of one seed block or of the 281-day test.

\textbf{Mechanism (exploratory, SENS-001).} Greedy, uniform and Leitner
share the same daily capacity, so their mean review day is identical
(14.065). Greedy gave the hardest third of items (shortest initial
half-life) 5.33 reviews on average and the easiest third 2.71, against 4
and 4 for uniform; its mean last-review day (23.98) was slightly earlier
than uniform's (24.18). Its gain therefore comes from moving reviews to
hard items, not from placing reviews closer to the test. Expanding and
massed end every item on the last session (day 27); expanding beats
uniform and massed does not, so late placement alone does not explain
the expanding gain either.

(The paired t p-value of the massed contrast underflows to 0 in double
precision, so the analysis records 0; the true value is positive and
very small.)

H0a is rejected: with the true model, greedy beats uniform. H0b is not
rejected and its bootstrap interval lies inside ±0.02. Under the frozen
interpretation rule, \textbf{the EXP-001 greedy advantage is declared
dependent on model knowledge.} The misspecification was effective: the
calibration error of \texttt{greedy-exp} was 0.1804, against 0 for the
oracle.

\textbf{Fragility of the equivalence classification (second review pass;
exploratory).} Three observations qualify this verdict without changing
it. First, the paired t interval of the same contrast, the protocol's
cross-check, reaches 0.0201, just outside the margin; the bootstrap
interval was the pre-fixed decision interval, but the classification
sits on the boundary. Second, on the independent seeds of SENS-001 the
same contrast is 0.0098 {[}0.0007, 0.0187{]}, an interval entirely above
0. Third, on the confirmatory learners, at retention intervals of 7 and
30 days, \texttt{greedy-exp} minus uniform is 0.0213 {[}0.0110,
0.0313{]} and 0.0213 {[}0.0109, 0.0314{]}. The stable finding is
quantitative: misspecification cut the greedy advantage on power-law
learners from 0.0347 to 0.0085 (about three quarters), leaving a small
positive difference near 0.01 whose classification as ``equivalent'' or
``above zero'' depends on the seed block and the retention interval.

\textbf{Non-adaptive arms win on power-law learners.} Massed (0.0530)
and expanding (0.0399) beat uniform by more than either greedy arm.
Massed, the worst arm in EXP-001, is the best arm here (mean \(R\)
0.7236 against 0.7053 for greedy-power and 0.6706 for uniform). Under a
power law, recall decays slowly at long delays, so the time from the
last review to the test matters more than which items are reviewed.

\textbf{The ranking is not stable.} Against the EXP-001 order (greedy,
expanding, uniform, leitner, massed), 70 of 72 cells reverse at least
one pair. The two forgetting models behave differently: under the power
law the top arm was massed in 24 of 36 cells; under exponential
forgetting the top arm was greedy or expanding in 14 cells each
(SENS-001, from the frozen cell means).

\textbf{Greedy below uniform.} The greedy minus uniform interval lies
entirely below 0 in 13 cells, all at the smallest budget (\(k = 2\)): 10
power-law cells, and the three exponential cells at \(RI = 281\)
(homogeneous -0.0090 {[}-0.0107, -0.0074{]}, lognormal -0.0444
{[}-0.0487, -0.0402{]}, bimodal -0.0698 {[}-0.0725, -0.0668{]}). A
plausible mechanism, measured only at the central cell (section 6), is
that with two reviews per item the extra reviews greedy gives hard items
leave some easy items with a single review; this was not measured at
\(k = 2\).

\textbf{Central cells.} C044 (exponential) reproduces the EXP-001 order
on independent seeds (greedy minus uniform 0.0167 {[}0.0113, 0.0218{]});
C045 (power law) gives massed first, as EXP-002 did (greedy minus
uniform 0.0417 {[}0.0307, 0.0524{]}).

\textbf{Expectations.} E1 holds in 13 of 18 groups; its five failures
are all power-law groups (budget 4 with homogeneous and lognormal items;
budget 8 with all three distributions), where massed beats uniform at
every \(RI\) but not monotonically. E2 holds in 16 of 24 groups; seven
of its eight failures are power-law groups.

\textbf{Robustness of the instability (exploratory, SENS-001).} The
70-cell count uses point estimates, and 16 cells (15 exponential, 1
power-law) have a uniform baseline above 0.95, where differences are
tiny. Counting a reversal only when the reversed pairwise difference has
a 95\% bootstrap interval that excludes 0 still gives 70 of 72 cells;
without the 16 ceiling cells, 54 of 56. The top arm is separated from
every other arm by such an interval in 59 of 72 cells (massed 28, greedy
15, expanding 14, uniform 2). The instability is not an artefact of
noise or of the ceiling.

\section{6. Discussion}\label{discussion}

\textbf{What the evidence supports.} Within these models, a scheduler
that knows the true model and each item's initial half-life, and reviews
the items with the lowest predicted recall, gives a small gain in mean
recall over equal spacing at the central setting. The gain replicates on
two independent seed blocks and at shorter retention intervals. Its
mechanism, visible in the exploratory diagnostics, is reallocation: hard
items get more reviews and easy items fewer. That mechanism also
explains its costs. Mastery share falls to 0, consistent with easy
items, the only ones that could stay above 0.9 after 281 days, losing
reviews. At two reviews per item the same reallocation plausibly becomes
harmful (13 cells below uniform, all at \(k = 2\)), although the
allocation was measured only at the central cell.

\textbf{Model knowledge.} The pre-stated invalidation test asked whether
the advantage survives a wrong model. It mostly does not: with an
exponential model on power-law learners the gain fell from 0.0347 to
0.0085, and the frozen rule classified it as equivalent to uniform. The
classification is fragile (section 5.2), but the size of the drop is
not. Both greedy arms still received each item's true initial half-life,
which no deployed scheduler has; the remaining advantage is an upper
bound on what a real scheduler with this model family could gain.

\textbf{Competing explanations.} The protocols named three for EXP-001
and one for EXP-002; Table 6 states which the evidence addresses.

\textbf{Retention interval and forgetting model.} The arm that wins
depends on the forgetting model more than on anything else. Under
exponential forgetting, recency matters little at long retention
intervals and targeting pays; under the power law, the slow tail makes
the time from the last review to the test decisive, and massed review
wins in two thirds of the cells. This is consistent in direction with
the report in the abstract of Cepeda et al.~(2006) that the best spacing
depends on the retention interval, but MEMORY's models contain no
spacing mechanism of the kind studied in human experiments (a review's
effect does not depend on the gap), so the agreement is not evidence for
either.

\textbf{Practical significance.} The largest confirmatory effect is a
few hundredths of a recall probability for a simulated learner. Since
neither model predicts real first-review recall better than a constant,
these magnitudes say nothing about human learners. What transfers is
methodological, and only as a caution: evaluating a model-based
scheduler on learners simulated from its own model can overstate its
advantage (here by a factor of about four at the central power-law
setting, 0.0347 against 0.0085), and a single setting can produce a
ranking that most nearby settings reverse.

\section{7. Limitations and threats to
validity}\label{limitations-and-threats-to-validity}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Construct validity.} Recall is a model probability, never a
  human measurement. Neither forgetting model beats a constant predictor
  of held-out real first-review recall (CAL-002). The calibration fixes
  the time scale of the simulated items, not the shape of forgetting.
\item
  \textbf{Model mechanics.} The retrieval update ignores the gap since
  the last review, so the models contain no spacing effect in the
  psychological sense; ``spacing'' here acts only through review success
  and recency.
\item
  \textbf{Information advantage.} Both greedy arms know each item's true
  initial half-life; EXP-001's greedy also knows the true model.
\item
  \textbf{Load confound.} Expanding and massed concentrate all reviews
  on 4 sessions (peak 50 per session); the other arms use 27 sessions
  (peak 8). Budgets are equal; daily burden is not. The Leitner arm is
  forced to the same fixed daily capacity as greedy, which may explain
  part of its deficit.
\item
  \textbf{Setting dependence.} The central retention interval (281 days)
  was chosen to move the baseline off the ceiling; it is a design
  choice, not a typical use case. \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\omega\)
  are planning values, and robustness to \(\omega\) is untested (D-017).
\item
  \textbf{Fragile classification.} The EXP-002 ``equivalent within
  0.02'' verdict sits on the margin and does not replicate on
  independent seeds or shorter retention intervals (exploratory).
\item
  \textbf{Pre-freeze exposure.} Draft-setting contrasts with the
  opposite sign were seen before the freeze (disclosed in the freeze
  record); the frozen setting was set by rules, not by these values.
\item
  \textbf{Statistics.} EXP-003 has 288 unadjusted arm-versus-uniform
  intervals; no single cell supports a confirmatory statement. Observed
  (Bernoulli) recall is noisier than \(R\) and its EXP-001 interval
  contains 0. E1 and E2 are judged on point estimates, and E2 compares
  signed differences, which reads oddly where greedy is below uniform in
  every distribution.
\item
  \textbf{Exploratory checks.} SENS-001 was specified after the results
  were seen; its thresholds (for example the 0.95 ceiling) are post hoc.
\item
  \textbf{Population.} The calibration data are Duolingo learners and
  words from 2013; they represent no other population.
\end{itemize}

\section{8. Ethics and responsible
research}\label{ethics-and-responsible-research}

No human participant was recruited and no user data was collected. The
only real data is DS01, used under its CC BY-NC 4.0 licence with
attribution; it holds pseudonymous learner identifiers, is not
redistributed (the file is git-ignored) and only aggregate fitted values
are committed. No ethics approval was sought, because none was required
for this design. The results must not be used to claim that any schedule
improves human learning, or to rank commercial products; no proprietary
algorithm was studied. A study of human learners would need its own
owner-approved review and safeguards.

\section{9. Conclusion and future
work}\label{conclusion-and-future-work}

In a budget-matched simulation of published forgetting models, a
model-based greedy scheduler beats equal spacing at one calibrated
setting by a small margin, mainly when it knows the true model, and at
the cost of item-level mastery. Across 72 settings no schedule is best
in general; massed review, the negative control of the central
experiment, is the most frequent winner, mostly under power-law
forgetting and at a daily load (50 reviews per session) that the other
arms never reach. The study's answer to ``which schedule maximizes
recall'' is therefore conditional: on the forgetting model, the budget,
the retention interval and the scheduler's knowledge. Feasible
extensions are a scheduler that learns item half-lives from outcomes
instead of receiving them, the untested \(\omega\) check, a load-matched
variant of the expanding and massed arms, and a memory model that fits
real first-review recall better than a constant.

\section{10. Data and code
availability}\label{data-and-code-availability}

All code, frozen protocols, configurations, results (except the
git-ignored 15.5 MB EXP-003 raw file, which the run command regenerates)
and reports are in the project repository, at a URL to be added on
release
(\texttt{\textless{}REPOSITORY\ URL:\ unpublished\textgreater{}}).
Reproduction: \texttt{uv\ sync\ -\/-frozen}, then
\texttt{uv\ run\ python\ -m\ memory\_research\ run\ -\/-config\ research/experiments/EXP-00N/config.json\ -\/-report\ -\/-pdf}
for N = 1, 2, 3, then \texttt{scripts/analyse\_confirmatory.py}; the
exploratory checks run with
\texttt{.venv/bin/python\ scripts/m4\_sensitivity.py}. Experiment
reports: \texttt{research/experiments/EXP-00N/report.md}. DS01 is
downloaded by \texttt{scripts/download\_duolingo.py} from its Dataverse
DOI and checked against \texttt{data/manifest.json}.

\section{11. Funding, competing interests and AI
assistance}\label{funding-competing-interests-and-ai-assistance}

No funding was received. The author declares no competing interests. An
AI system (Claude, Anthropic) was used as a research and development
assistant: it drafted protocols, code, analysis scripts and
documentation under the author's direction. The author approved every
protocol freeze and amendment. All numbers were generated by committed
code from committed results, and an automated cross-check of every
decimal number in the manuscript and reports against those results was
run (\texttt{research/publication/evidence\_audit.md}). The AI's
internal review is quality control, not external peer review; this
manuscript has not been peer-reviewed.
